items.key: being you: a new science of consciousness
items.text: The author's own book expanding on the argument that life matters for consciousness, referenced for fuller treatment.
items.context: Being You: A New Science of Consciousness

items.key: frankenstein
items.text: Used as a cultural example of the long, mostly unhappy history of synthetic consciousness stories.
items.context: Frankenstein

items.key: 2001: a space odyssey
items.text: Cited as a cultural touchstone (HAL 9000) for synthetic minds that think and feel going wrong.
items.context: 2001: A Space Odyssey

items.key: ex machina
items.text: Used repeatedly as an example (Ava, Caleb, Nathan) illustrating the temptation and testing of machine consciousness, source of the 'Garland test'.
items.context: Ex Machina

items.key: klara and the sun
items.text: Cited as another cultural example of a synthetic mind narrative.
items.context: Klara and the Sun

items.key: yossele the golem
items.text: Cited as the earliest cultural example of the dream of creating artificial synthetic beings.
items.context: Yossele the Golem

items.key: interview claiming lamda is conscious
items.text: Cited as an early high-profile claim that an AI chatbot was conscious, sparking the debate the essay addresses.
items.context: Interview claiming LaMDA is conscious

items.key: suggestion that conscious machines may be possible in the near future
items.text: Cited as a leading thinker suggesting machine consciousness may soon be possible.
items.context: Suggestion that conscious machines may be possible in the near future

items.key: claim that conscious ai already exists
items.text: Cited as an AI pioneer who believes conscious machines already exist, used as example of overattribution.
items.context: Claim that conscious AI already exists

items.key: article on the need to take ai welfare seriously
items.text: Cited as evidence that serious researchers are now considering the moral status of AI systems.
items.context: Article on the need to take AI welfare seriously

items.key: what is it like to be a bat?
items.text: Provides the definition of consciousness as 'something it is like to be' an organism, central to the essay's argument.
items.context: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

items.key: more everything forever
items.text: Describes the projection of consciousness onto AI as pareidolia, a concept the essay adopts.
items.context: More Everything Forever

items.key: turing machine / universal computation formalism
items.text: Provides the foundational definition of computation the essay uses to argue brains are not computers.
items.context: Turing machine / universal computation formalism

items.key: a logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity
items.text: Landmark paper showing networks of abstract neurons can perform logical operations, foundation of neural network computation.
items.context: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity

items.key: work demonstrating turing completeness of neural networks
items.text: Showed artificial neural networks with memory are Turing complete, supporting the brain-as-computer metaphor the essay challenges.
items.context: Work demonstrating Turing completeness of neural networks

items.key: research on neurons firing spikes to clear metabolic waste
items.text: Empirical finding used to argue silicon cannot perfectly replace biological neurons because of embedded metabolic functions.
items.context: Research on neurons firing spikes to clear metabolic waste

items.key: remark on confusing a metaphor with the thing itself
items.text: Provides the philosophical caution against mistaking the brain-as-computer metaphor for reality.
items.context: Remark on confusing a metaphor with the thing itself

items.key: what might cognition be, if not computation?
items.text: Introduces the Watt governor example used to argue some systems are better understood non-computationally.
items.context: What Might Cognition Be, If Not Computation?

items.key: biological naturalism (view that life properties are necessary for consciousness)
items.text: Provides the philosophical position, biological naturalism, that the essay draws on to argue life matters for consciousness.
items.context: Biological naturalism (view that life properties are necessary for consciousness)

items.key: are you living in a computer simulation?
items.text: Source of the simulation hypothesis, critiqued for assuming without argument that computation is sufficient for consciousness.
items.context: Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?

items.key: lectures on ethics
items.text: Cited for the argument that treating conscious-seeming things as if they lack consciousness is psychologically unhealthy.
items.context: Lectures on Ethics

items.key: comments on the dangers of conscious-seeming ai
items.text: Cited as a leading AI figure who has started to notice the dangers of conscious-seeming AI.
items.context: Comments on the dangers of conscious-seeming AI

items.key: comments on the dangers of conscious-seeming ai
items.text: Cited alongside Suleyman as noticing the dangers posed by conscious-seeming AI systems.
items.context: Comments on the dangers of conscious-seeming AI

items.key: description of ai as a mirror reflecting our digitized past
items.text: Provides the mirror metaphor used to close the essay's argument about mistaking algorithms for ourselves.
items.context: Description of AI as a mirror reflecting our digitized past

items.key: remark that technology can make us forget what we know about life
items.text: Closing quote used to reinforce the essay's call to remember our embodied, living nature.
items.context: Remark that technology can make us forget what we know about life
